# India's Wide-Body Window

> Where should Indian carriers deploy their next 100 long-haul aircraft, and can the India-Gulf corridor absorb them? A commercial aviation market entry case built on DGCA, Eurostat, IATA and World Bank data. The answer: compete with the Gulf hubs, do not fly more aircraft to them. Europe first, North America second, Gulf capacity roughly flat.

Author: Anklesh Rawat. Licence: Apache-2.0. Published 2026.
Canonical: https://india-widebody-window.vercel.app
Mirror: https://doginfantry.github.io/india-widebody-window/
Source and data: https://github.com/DogInfantry/india-widebody-window

Every figure below is computed inside the repository from committed data, or carries a
source URL and pull date in the data dictionary. Modelled figures are labelled as modelled
on the chart face and a test fails the build if one is published without that label. Where
two agencies disagree the conflict is reported rather than resolved away. The analysis
changed direction ten times and each change is written up with the commit it happened in.

## The answer

Compete with the Gulf hubs. Do not fly more aircraft to them.

The India-Gulf corridor carries 50.9% of India's international sector traffic, 39.7M
passengers in 2025, and is 4.1 times the size of India's entire direct Europe market. It is
still the wrong place to put a wide-body, for three separate reasons. About 8.5M of those
passengers a year are not going to the Gulf at all, they are connecting through Dubai, Doha
or Abu Dhabi to somewhere else. The treaty room left at the two Gulf points with a published
entitlement would absorb about 4% of the aircraft on firm order. And Gulf sectors are short
enough that unit cost stays high, so the Gulf is the only corridor that cannot cover its own
cost at IndiGo's achieved yield. Indian carriers win that traffic by flying past the Gulf,
not to it: Europe first, North America second, Gulf capacity roughly flat.

## Key figures

- India international sector passengers, both directions, all carriers, 2025: 78.0M. Computed from DGCA.
- Share of that traffic touching a Gulf point, 2025: 50.9%, which is 39.7M passengers. Computed from DGCA.
- Share flown by Indian carriers, 2025: 45.9%, against 26.2% for Gulf carriers. Computed from DGCA.
- Indian carrier share in 2015: 37.0%, against 32.7% for Gulf carriers. The premise reversed: Indian carriers are gaining, not losing.
- IndiGo international passengers, 2025: 16.7M, against Air India's 10.7M.
- IndiGo average international stage length, 2025: 2,643 km, against Air India's 5,316 km.
- Passengers a year connecting through a Gulf hub to somewhere else: 8.5M. Modelled, and bounded below at 7.84M by IATA measurement, so the modelled figure is slightly conservative.
- Firm wide-body order book: 140 aircraft, 80 Air India and 60 IndiGo, which is +78% on Indian carriers' current international capacity measured in ASK, and 1.94 times the growth needed to hold share.
- Share of that order book the remaining Gulf treaty room could absorb: about 4%.
- Yield headroom by corridor, 2025: Gulf -4.3%, South Asia -1.9%, East Asia +8.9%, Southeast Asia +11.2%, Africa +16.9%, Europe +21.3%, Oceania +29.5%, North America +31.5%.
- India international passengers in 2030: a band of 96M to 109M across three independent methods. Reported as a band and never as an average, because the spread is the useful output.
- India-Dubai seat entitlement already used: 88.8%. Abu Dhabi: 70.1%. The Gulf is not uniformly capped.
- Gulf share of corridor revenue: 31%, against 52% of passengers.
- IndiGo FY2026 EBITDAR margin: 17.8% as reported, and 27.3% excluding foreign exchange. Both figures must be read together or neither means anything.
- Coverage of the target job posting: 82%, not 100%, and the missing items are named rather than engineered away.

## Definitions that change the answer

- Sector traffic counts a passenger on each leg. Origin-destination counts where the passenger is actually going. The Gulf is 50.9% of sectors and roughly 40% of origin-destination, and the eleven point gap is the connecting passenger. That gap is the case, not a discrepancy.
- Capacity is measured in ASK, available seat kilometres, never in seats or aircraft. A seat is not capacity until you say how far and how often it flies, and this case turns on how far.
- DGCA sums both directions and reports on a fiscal year. IATA counts departures only and reports on a calendar year. Comparing the wrong pair doubles the connect gap.

## Sources

- DGCA traffic statistics, via the community mirror at github.com/Vonter/india-aviation-traffic, ODbL. Five datasets, fresh to May 2026, pulled 2026-08-15. The spine of the analysis.
- Eurostat avia_par, EU reuse policy. The European end of India-Europe routes, used to check DGCA from the opposite direction. The two agree to 2.6% across seven countries.
- IATA, Aviation in India, free publication. India's departing international origin-destination split by region and by country. Route level data is a separate paid product.
- World Bank Open Data, CC BY 4.0. Income, population and air travel propensity across twelve peer countries.
- OurAirports, CC0. Airport reference data and coordinates.

## What would make this wrong

The softest input is the Gulf six origin-destination share. No agency publishes it, so it is
gated as unverifiable, corroborated at region level and bounded by measurement, and it is
still the likeliest reason the recommendation fails. Wide-body lease rates are the largest
unquantified cost and no free primary exists for them. Route level cross-checking against a
second agency covers only 5.6% of India's international traffic, all of it Europe, because
no Gulf authority publishes route statistics.
